title: ITA Section 37(1): SR&ED Expenditure Pool Legislation
description: Explore Canada's ITA Section 37(1) legislation on the SR&ED expenditure pool. Learn how Canadian businesses deduct and carry forward eligible R&D expenses.
summary: Subsection 37(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act creates a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada. Current expenditures, and capital expenditures restored after December 15, 2024, reduce net income, and any unused balance carries forward indefinitely, while SR&ED investment tax credits claimed reduce the pool the following year.

body.text: Subsection 37(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act creates a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures for taxpayers carrying on business in Canada. Current expenditures, and capital expenditures restored after December 15, 2024, reduce net income, and any unused balance carries forward indefinitely, while SR&ED investment tax credits claimed reduce the pool the following year.
Executive Overview and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Tax Law

Canada maintains one of the most comprehensive and mature fiscal frameworks for industrial innovation in the developed world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly through policy formulation by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the federal SR&ED regime functions as a dual-mechanism tax incentive codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Rather than operating as a discretionary subsidy, the SR&ED framework establishes a statutory entitlement whereby any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs technically qualifying research and experimental development within Canadian territorial jurisdiction—or permissible supporting salary activities outside Canada—is legally entitled to both an immediate or indefinitely deferrable income deduction and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC).

The statutory architecture rests upon two distinct but interconnected pillars of the Income Tax Act that govern income computation and tax credit generation. The first pillar is the Subsection 37(1) Deductible Expenditure Pool, through which section 37 of the ITA overrides the general capital prohibition of paragraph 18(1)(b) by establishing a dedicated, cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer may deduct current SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a)—as well as eligible SR&ED capital expenditures restored for acquisitions occurring after December 15, 2024—to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year. Any unutilized balance remaining in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool does not expire at year-end; rather, it carries forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years at the taxpayer's discretion.

The second pillar is the Subsection 127(5) and 127(9) Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Regime, under which section 127 of the ITA converts "qualified expenditures" defined in subsection 127(9) into direct reductions of federal Part I tax payable or, for qualifying corporations, direct cash refunds. While the subsection 37(1) deduction pool measures actual cash outlays and incurred liabilities deductible against corporate income, the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base incorporates specific statutory adjustments. Most notably, subsection 127(9) permits the inclusion of a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead calculated under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, while enforcing statutory restrictions on non-arm's-length transfers, used equipment, and government or non-government assistance under subsection 127(18). Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs earned in a taxation year may be carried back three taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable.

body.text: This statutory division between the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) credit pool creates an intricate structural dynamic for Canadian corporate tax planning. When a claimant deducts SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) in Year 1 and earns an SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(5), the ITC claimed—whether received as a cash refund or applied as an offset against Part I tax payable—is subtracted from the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year. This triggers a mandatory reduction of the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in Year 2 under paragraph 37(1)(e), or a direct income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(v) to the extent that the reductions exceed the available pool balance. Consequently, the net effective fiscal benefit of the SR&ED program is an interdependent function of federal corporate tax rates, current-year provincial R&D tax credit assistance reductions, and the claimant's annual election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method.
The 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul: Consultations, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15

Between January 2024 and March 2026, Canada executed the most consequential structural modernization of the SR&ED program since the 2012–2014 federal reforms. For more than a decade following the 2012 budget amendments—which had eliminated capital expenditures and capital lease costs from SR&ED eligibility, lowered the general corporate ITC rate from 20% to 15%, discounted arm's-length contract payments to 80%, and stepped down the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate from 65% in 2012 to 60% in 2013 and 55% from 2014 onward—industry groups and tax practitioners argued that the program's statutory parameters penalized capital-intensive R&D, prematurely stripped scaling technology enterprises of the enhanced 35% credit, and excluded innovative domestic public companies.
The Two-Phase Department of Finance Consultation Process (2024)

On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada formally launched Phase One of its public consultation on the SR&ED program, which ran until April 15, 2024. The Department's consultation paper solicited technical submissions across seven foundational policy inquiries designed to recalibrate Canada's innovation ecosystem. Specifically, the government examined how the SR&ED program could remain effective in supporting R&D investment across businesses of all sizes and better support the growth and scaling of R&D-intensive Canadian enterprises, as well as what statutory modifications to the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, eligibility criteria, or overall program architecture should be enacted. Furthermore, the consultation evaluated how the SR&ED tax incentive could achieve greater complementarity with Canada's existing suite of direct grant and contribution programs, and whether overall assistance levels within the program could be more effectively targeted. A central policy concern raised in the consultation paper was how the SR&ED regime could ensure the retention of intellectual property (IP) within Canada so that innovative firms remain Canadian-owned and operated, alongside administrative inquiries into how CRA filing and audit procedures could be streamlined for entrepreneurs and how enhancements could be funded to maximize economic opportunities for Canadians.

Following the tabling of Federal Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance on April 16, 2024, the federal government launched Phase Two of the SR&ED consultations, which remained open for stakeholder submissions until May 27, 2024. This two-stage consultative process directly shaped the legislative reforms announced in the late-2024 fiscal update and Federal Budget 2025.
Enactment of Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and Retroactive Application

The legislative culmination of the 2024 consultations and subsequent Budget 2025 announcements occurred on March 26, 2026, when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent. Although formally enacted in March 2026, the substantive statutory enhancements to corporate expenditure limits, taxable capital phase-out ranges, public corporation eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, taxation years commencing on or after December 16, 2024) and to capital property acquisitions and equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024. To operationalize Bill C-15, the CRA released updated prescribed forms on May 15, 2026—specifically the revised Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) and Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length)—followed on May 22, 2026 by the updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy and the revised SR&ED Total Qualified Expenditure Policy.

body.text: The structural economic implications of Bill C-15 are profound for scaling industrial and technology ventures. Under the pre-December 16, 2024 rules, Canadian venture-backed technology, clean-tech, and life sciences companies that closed a Series B or Series C equity financing round routinely breached the $10 million taxable capital threshold—because issued share capital and long-term debt liabilities, net of accumulated deficits, expand taxable capital employed in Canada—thereby eroding their $3 million expenditure limit and entirely eliminating access to the 35% refundable credit once prior-year taxable capital reached $50 million. Similarly, domestic growth companies that executed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange automatically forfeited their Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) status upon listing, dropping overnight from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit. By doubling the annual expenditure limit to $6 million, elevating the prior-year taxable capital phase-out window to $15 million–$75 million, and extending the 35% enhanced credit rate to eligible Canadian public corporations, Parliament removed the fiscal penalty previously imposed on domestic public listings and late-stage domestic equity capitalization.
Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Phase-Out Mechanics
The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates as a two-tiered rate regime governed by subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act.
The General 15% Rate Versus the Enhanced 35% Rate

The baseline federal SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada. This general 15% rate applies to foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, individuals (sole proprietorships), trusts, and partnerships, as well as to the portion of a qualifying CCPC's or eligible Canadian public corporation's qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds its annual expenditure limit. For corporate claimants, the 15% basic ITC is non-refundable and may only be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax payable, with any unutilized credit balance eligible to be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years.

In contrast, qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations earn an enhanced ITC at the rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Furthermore, a qualifying CCPC earns 100% cash refundability on the 35% ITC generated from its current SR&ED expenditures and its Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) within its annual expenditure limit. This 100% cash refundability transforms the SR&ED program into a critical non-dilutive working capital engine for pre-revenue and loss-making CCPC startups that have no Part I corporate income tax payable.
Mathematical Mechanics of the Subsection 127(10.2) Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit across an associated corporate group is $6,000,000. Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, this $6 million ceiling is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (and its associated corporations') taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, phasing out completely once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. Specifically, subsection 127(10.2) establishes the statutory expenditure limit formula as follows:

In this statutory equation, the variable A represents the prior-year taxable capital reduction factor. Where the corporation's (and associated group's) taxable capital employed in Canada in the preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less, the variable A is nil ($0), which yields the full statutory expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the variable A equals the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000 (capped at $60,000,000), meaning that every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the corporation's $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. Once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $75,000,000 or more, the variable A equals $60,000,000, reducing the numerator ($60,000,000 − A) to zero and resulting in an expenditure limit of $0. Any qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a corporation above its phased-out expenditure limit remain fully eligible for the basic 15% ITC rate. By comparison, for taxation years that began before December 16, 2024, the legacy subsection 127(10.2) formula utilized a $3,000,000 base limit and phased out over a much narrower prior-year taxable capital corridor of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Specified Employee Caps, and Restoration of Capital and Lease Costs

Only specific categories of expenditures enumerated in section 37 of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations qualify for inclusion in the SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC calculation. Every claimed expenditure must be incurred in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada—subject to the limited statutory allowance for foreign salary—and must be related to a business carried on by the claimant.
Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Labour, Support Staff, and Specified Employees

Salaries and wages typically constitute the largest expenditure category in Canadian SR&ED claims. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" is strictly defined as income from an office or employment as computed under sections 5, 6, and 7 of the Act. Consequently, dividends paid to shareholder-founders do not constitute salary or wages and are completely ineligible for SR&ED, nor can a corporation claim any notional expenditure for the unpaid labour of founders who draw no payroll remuneration during the taxation year.

The eligibility of employee remuneration depends directly on the overhead calculation method elected by the claimant on Form T661. When a claimant elects the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), only the portion of salaries or wages of employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada may be included in the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the proxy salary base. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" is determined by the hands-on technical nature of their tasks—such as conducting experiments, fabricating prototypes, writing experimental source code, or providing first-line direct technical supervision—rather than their corporate title. Salaries of employees who support SR&ED indirectly, such as clerical staff, human resources, accounting, or purchasing personnel, cannot be claimed on Form T661 under the proxy method because their cost is statutorily deemed to be encompassed within the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Conversely, when a claimant chooses the Traditional Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), the corporation may claim the salaries or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED, and may also claim administrative salaries or wages that are directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures.

Under both overhead methods—and specifically governed by subsection 2900(5) of the Regulations for the proxy method—the All or Substantially All (ASA) rule provides that if an employee spends 90% or more of their employment time during the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be allocated to SR&ED. Where an employee spends less than 90% of their working time on SR&ED, only the reasonable proportion of their salary or wages attributable to SR&ED, substantiated by contemporaneous time-tracking and labour allocation evidence, may be included. Furthermore, pursuant to section 10.0 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees may be included in the claim, provided the work is directly undertaken in support of and forms an integral part of a core SR&ED project carried on in Canada, up to a statutory ceiling of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid for work performed in Canada.

With respect to variable compensation and fringe benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and inducement or non-competition payments deemed to be employment remuneration may be included in deductible SR&ED salary or wages solely for non-specified employees. Taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA may also be included in SR&ED salary or wages where there is a cash outlay for the benefit or, in the case of a non-cash benefit, where the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes any Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) or Provincial Sales Tax (PST) for which an input tax credit is available, and the underlying cost is not separately deducted as a business expense. However, all bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, inducement payments, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year under subsection 78(4) are strictly excluded from the proxy salary base for every employee under subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations.
Statutory Restrictions on Specified Employees (Owner-Managers and Founders)

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce stringent anti-avoidance caps on specified employees to prevent closely held corporations from inflating refundable SR&ED tax credits through discretionary year-end owner-manager compensation. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee is an employee who is a specified shareholder of the corporation—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any corporation related to it, counting shares owned by persons who do not deal at arm's length with the individual—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer.

Specified employees are governed by three mandatory statutory restrictions across the SR&ED expenditure pool and the proxy salary base. First, under subsection 37(9) of the ITA (reported on Line 305 of Form T661 per Guide T4088), a corporation is strictly barred from including any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee in its SR&ED expenditures. While such a bonus remains deductible as a general corporate payroll expense under subsection 9(1), it generates neither a subsection 37(1) SR&ED deduction pool addition nor a subsection 127(9) SR&ED tax credit.

Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a single specified employee in a taxation year cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) established under the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. Under subsections 37(9.2) to (9.4), if a specified employee is employed by multiple associated corporations, this single 5 × YMPE ceiling must be allocated across the associated group. For calendar year 2026, where the CPP YMPE is $74,600, the maximum SR&ED salary cap for a specified employee employed for the full 365-day taxation year is $373,000 (5 × $74,600).

Third, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations imposes a second, lower ceiling that restricts the amount of a specified employee's salary eligible to enter the salary base to earn the 55% PPA. Specifically, the proxy salary base inclusion for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the corporation for the year (encompassing both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year under s. 78(4)), or 2.5 × A × B/365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends and B is the number of days in the tax year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days during the year that the employee was not a specified employee). Under subsection 2900(8) of the Regulations, associated corporations employing the same specified employee must share a single 2.5 × YMPE proxy base limit across the corporate group. For calendar year 2026 (YMPE of $74,600), the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base ceiling equals $186,500.

body.text: The mathematical interplay between subsection 37(9.1) and Regulation 2900(7) creates a vital payroll planning consideration for technical founders. If a founder-CEO owns 50% of a startup's shares, draws a $100,000 regular payroll salary with no bonus, and spends 70% of the year directly engaged in SR&ED, the corporation may include $70,000 of SR&ED salary—below both the subsection 37(9.1) ceiling and the Regulation 2900(7) proxy base ceiling—and, under the Proxy Method, generate a $38,500 PPA ($70,000 × 55%), yielding $108,500 in qualified expenditures and $37,975 in refundable federal ITC ($108,500 × 35%) per founder.
Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Costs

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Income Tax Act (Proxy Method), a claimant may deduct in its section 37 pool and include in its qualified expenditure base the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass physical supplies and inputs that are destroyed, exhausted, or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials, prototyping, or laboratory testing. Materials transformed encompass raw materials and components integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant that are converted into another product or physical state during the SR&ED investigation, subject to statutory ITC recapture rules if the resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use. In contemporary software engineering, data science, and artificial intelligence (AI) research, cloud computing costs—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure environments—as well as dedicated GPU compute resources utilized directly for SR&ED activities like training and testing experimental machine learning models, are recognized as eligible SR&ED expenditures (claimed as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED or directly attributable overhead/equipment lease costs depending on the contractual structure and dedicated usage), provided commercial production hosting costs are strictly segregated and excluded.
Subcontractors and Third-Party SR&ED Contracts

Payments made to third-party contractors that perform eligible SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf qualify under paragraph 37(1)(a), subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) of the ITA. Where the work is contracted to an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) SR&ED pool, whereas only 80% of the arm's-length contract expenditure is included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) for the purpose of calculating the SR&ED ITC—a statutory discounting rule designed to strip out the subcontractor's presumed profit markup and prevent cascading credits. Where SR&ED work is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length party, the contract payment itself does not qualify for ITCs in the hands of the payer; instead, the non-arm's-length parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (reported on Line 540 of the performer's Form T661) to the payer.
Restoration of SR&ED Capital and Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

A cornerstone of the Bill C-15 legislative overhaul (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the statutory restoration of SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Expenditures for depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024, or equipment lease outlays incurred before December 16, 2024, remain completely ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives.

An eligible SR&ED capital expenditure is defined as an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property that becomes available for use after December 15, 2024, is used for SR&ED carried out in Canada related to the claimant's business, and is intended at the time of acquisition to be used all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed in performing SR&ED in Canada. If a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024 and straddles that effective date, the claimant must calculate SR&ED usage as a percentage of total operating time during the period after December 15, 2024. Land and leasehold interests in land are statutorily excluded under paragraph 37(1)(b), and buildings and leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings) are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e), so they do not qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures. Moreover, while capital expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for used equipment (entered on Line 390 of Form T661) are included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, used equipment is excluded from "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) and therefore does not qualify for the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Claimants must also monitor downstream dispositions: selling SR&ED capital property or converting it to commercial use triggers both an SR&ED ITC recapture and a Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) recapture.

For equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, eligibility and reporting on Form T661 depend on the equipment's SR&ED operating time percentage and the claimant's overhead election. Where leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the post-December 15, 2024 lease cost is claimed on Line 350 of Form T661 under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. Where leased equipment is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of the time) for SR&ED, a claimant electing the Proxy Method may claim 50% of the lease cost on Line 355 of Form T661, provided the leased asset is not general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF). Conversely, a claimant electing the Traditional Method enters "0" on Line 355 and instead claims the actual SR&ED-attributable share of post-December 15, 2024 lease costs for equipment used less than 90% of the time on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures.
Overhead Calculation Methods: The Traditional Method Versus the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

Subsections 37(8) and 37(10) of the Income Tax Act require every SR&ED claimant to make an annual election on Form T661 between two mutually exclusive approaches for accounting for SR&ED overhead and indirect supporting expenditures: the Proxy Method (elected on Line 160 under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (chosen on Line 162 under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Under subsection 37(10), the proxy election must be filed on the day the claimant first files Form T661 for the year, and once made the election is irrevocable for the taxation year.
Comprehensive Comparison of the Traditional and Proxy Methods

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant must specifically identify, track, and substantiate every actual overhead and supporting expenditure that is directly attributable (meaning directly related and incremental, per subsection 2900(2) of the Income Tax Regulations) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, reporting those actual overhead outlays on Line 360 of Form T661. These itemized overhead outlays—such as incremental utilities that vary with SR&ED usage, maintenance and repairs of SR&ED premises and equipment, and directly related clerical or purchasing support salaries—are included in both the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base that earns the ITC, whereas fixed maintenance contracts that do not vary with SR&ED usage are excluded.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant foregoes claiming actual overhead and indirect supporting salaries on Form T661, instead deducting its actual overhead outlays as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the ITA. In exchange, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations entitles the claimant to compute a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the salary base (reported on Line 502 in Part 5 of Form T661). Crucially, the PPA is included exclusively in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) for the purpose of generating the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit; the PPA cannot be added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations, the PPA is subject to an overall statutory cap whereby it cannot exceed the claimant's total business deductions for the taxation year less specified deductions and building costs.

body.text: Worked Comparative Financial Computation (Calendar 2026 Taxation Year)

To demonstrate the precise statutory mechanics of the Traditional versus Proxy election in 2026, consider a qualifying CCPC well below the $6,000,000 expenditure limit with a December 31, 2026 taxation year-end. During the 2026 taxation year, non-specified engineering employees directly engaged in SR&ED earned $300,000 in regular salary with no bonuses or taxable benefits. In addition, the founder-owner—a specified shareholder owning more than 10% of the corporation's shares—earned $200,000 in regular payroll salary and spent 80% of the year directly engaged in SR&ED, yielding $160,000 in direct SR&ED salary, which falls below the 2026 subsection 37(9.1) ceiling of $373,000. Under Regulation 2900(7), however, the founder's inclusion in the proxy salary base is restricted to the lesser of 75% of total salary ($150,000) and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500), capping the founder's proxy salary base contribution at $150,000. During the same period, the corporation consumed $30,000 of materials in SR&ED and incurred $150,000 in provable, directly related, and incremental SR&ED overhead that would qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method.

body.text: As this comparative computation confirms, unless a claimant's provable, incremental Line 360 overhead exceeds the 55% PPA generated by its eligible salary base ($247,500 vs. $150,000), the Proxy Method produces a substantially higher SR&ED Investment Tax Credit ($258,125 versus $224,000, a net cash refund advantage of $34,125) while simultaneously eliminating the compliance burden and audit exposure of tracking utility bills, maintenance logs, and support-staff time allocations. While the Traditional Method places $150,000 more into the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool ($640,000 vs. $490,000), the corporation electing the Proxy Method still deducts that $150,000 of actual overhead as an ordinary business expense under subsection 9(1) in computing its net income for the year.
Technological Eligibility Criteria, Judicial Precedents, and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

To qualify as Scientific Research and Experimental Development under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, work must consist of a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute divides eligible work into three core categories—(a) basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; (b) applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and (c) experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements—alongside (d) eligible support work, which encompasses engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude routine and commercial activities from SR&ED eligibility, including market research or sales promotion, quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes (paragraph (f)), research in the social sciences or the humanities, prospecting, exploring or drilling for or producing minerals, petroleum or natural gas, the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process, style changes, and routine data collection.
Foundational Canadian Jurisprudence: The Five-Question Test

Canadian judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) is anchored by a consistent line of Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence that remains binding law through 2026. In the foundational decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CarswellNat 696 (Tax Court of Canada), Judge Donald G.H. Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) evaluated CRA Information Circular IC 86-4R3. At paragraphs 13 through 15 of Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman observed that in light of the extensive consultation and the impressive credentials of the scientific panels involved in its drafting, IC 86-4R3 serves as a "generally useful and reliable guide" built around three fundamental criteria: scientific or technological uncertainty, scientific or technological content, and scientific or technological advancement. At paragraph 16 of the judgment, Justice Bowman formulated the definitive five-question test that Canadian courts and the CRA apply to determine whether a taxpayer's activities constitute SR&ED.

First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; if the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, which entails a five-stage methodology comprising the observation of the subject matter, the identification of the problem, the formulation of a hypothesis, the testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and the formulation of logical conclusions. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses. Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, meaning an advancement in general understanding; crucially, Justice Bowman established that the rejection of an unsuccessful hypothesis is itself a technological advancement if it eliminates an avenue of uncertainty and advances understanding of why an approach fails. Fifth, the court asks whether the taxpayer kept a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.

body.text: Subsequent appellate and trial decisions have refined how the fifth criterion—contemporaneous documentation—is weighed during tax litigation. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), Justice Robertson affirmed Northwest Hydraulic and clarified that while creating contemporaneous documentation with specific SR&ED intent is not a standalone statutory condition precedent to the recognition of SR&ED, a taxpayer seeking to establish on a balance of probabilities that systematic experimental testing occurred relies heavily on contemporaneous data, test logs, and records of hypotheses generated as the work progressed. In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, the Federal Court of Appeal cemented Justice Bowman's five-question test as the universal standard. More recently, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (TCC, 2025), the Tax Court of Canada allowed an informal-procedure appeal involving experimental food processing aimed at achieving a two-year room-temperature shelf life for unpasteurized cold-pressed juice without pasteurization, where early experimental batches caused cans to explode due to microbial growth releasing oxygen. Rejecting the Minister's contention that the taxpayer merely sought a routine shelf-life extension, the Court applied Justice Sommerfeldt's articulation of the scientific method, reiterated that "contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development," and held that the taxpayer proved on a balance of probabilities that its uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering. Conversely, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175, aff'g 2025 TCC 183, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the taxpayer's appeal, confirming that the Tax Court correctly applied the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as approved in RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies; the Tax Court had found that none of the projects had a hypothesis and that the records were inadequate, and the testimony of a credible, uncontradicted witness did not displace the Minister's assumptions of fact.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Multi-Jurisdictional Stackability
In addition to the federal SR&ED program, Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory maintain parallel corporate R&D tax incentives that stack on top of the federal ITC.
The Mechanics of Federal-Provincial Stackability ("Government Assistance")

When a corporation claims both a provincial R&D tax credit and the federal SR&ED ITC on the same underlying expenditures, the headline credit rates cannot simply be added together. Under paragraph 12(1)(x), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance. Consequently, the dollar amount of the provincial R&D tax credit earned in the current taxation year reduces both the federal subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the federal subsection 127(9) "qualified expenditures" base before the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate is applied. One technical exception governs claimants electing the Proxy Method: in provinces such as British Columbia and Ontario where the provincial R&D credit base includes the federal Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), the portion of the provincial tax credit arising from the notional PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, and specialized assistance adjustments on Schedule 31 and Schedule 508 prevent anomalous negative ITC calculations.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition and filed via the T2 corporate income tax return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations (CCPCs) with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure cap of $3,000,000 across an associated group. This $3 million expenditure limit phases out when the associated group's prior-year taxable capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. To receive the OITC, the corporation must file Schedule 566 alongside federal Form T661 within 18 months of the end of the taxation year. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit to any corporation with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures net of any OITC claimed (unless the corporation elects to waive the OITC). Unused ORDTC balances may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedules 568 and 569, provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified R&D contract expenditures incurred by a corporation under an eligible contract with an approved Ontario research institute.
Québec: The 2025 Abolition of Legacy Credits (Form RD-1029.7) and the New Unified CRIC Regime

Québec operates an autonomous corporate tax system administered by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec). In its 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Québec government enacted a sweeping structural consolidation of its R&D tax incentive landscape. For fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec's primary incentive was the refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) claimed on Form RD-1029.7 (supported by technical project form RD-222), which provided a base 14% refundable credit and an enhanced rate of up to 30% for qualifying SMEs on eligible Québec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor costs above an exclusion threshold, alongside separate credits for university or public research centre contracts, private partnership pre-competitive research, fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and technological adaptation services.

Effective for any corporation or qualified partnership whose taxation year or fiscal period begins after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished all five of those legacy tax credits: the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and the tax credit for technological adaptation services. Replacing the abolished regime, Québec instituted a unified refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (also referred to as the tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization, CRIC) (reported on the Québec corporate return CO-17, lines 440p to 440y, codes 112 and 113). This new Québec regime covers both R&D activities and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec across four eligible expenditure pillars—salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to certain research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property—at a base refundable rate of 20% (and an enhanced 30% rate on up to $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold).
British Columbia: BCRDTC (Form T666 / Schedule 425)

Under Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act, the British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit (BCRDTC) is claimed on Form T666 (Schedule 425) filed with the federal T2 return. Qualifying CCPCs and, for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations with a permanent establishment in British Columbia earn a 10% refundable tax credit on eligible BC SR&ED expenditures up to their expenditure limit, while other corporations and claimants with expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit that can be carried back 3 years or carried forward 10 years. Originally scheduled to expire on September 1, 2022, the BCRDTC was legislatively extended to September 1, 2027; the Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (Bill 2, S.B.C. 2026, c. 5) then removed the expiry date, making the credit permanent, and aligned it with federal Bill C-15 for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024 by raising the refundable expenditure limit to $6,000,000, widening the taxable capital phase-out to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, and incorporating eligible SR&ED capital expenditures incurred in British Columbia, with Schedule 425 updated for 2025 and 2026 accordingly.
Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (AT1 Schedule 29)

Alberta delivers its R&D incentive directly through the provincial corporate tax system via the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), overseen by the Ministry of Technology and Innovation and claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AS29) filed with the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1). Applicable to eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 (matching federal SR&ED qualified expenditures) up to an annual spending cap of $4,000,000, the IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending—calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years—and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on incremental eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's 2-year average base spending level. To target support toward small and medium-sized enterprises, the IEG phases out incrementally for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and corporations with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are ineligible.

body.text: Governing Authorities, Mandatory Tax Schedules, Administrative Pre-Approval, and Statutory Filing Deadlines
Governing Authorities and Single-Window Versus Dual-Window Administration

The administration of R&D tax incentives in Canada involves a division of institutional authority between federal and provincial revenue agencies. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program nationwide, as well as the harmonized provincial R&D tax credits of Ontario (Schedules 566, 508, 568, and 569), British Columbia (Schedule 425 / Form T666), Manitoba, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon through the single-window T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filing system. Within the CRA, SR&ED claims undergo bifurcated technical and financial examination: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) evaluate whether claimed projects satisfy the subsection 248(1) technological eligibility criteria and the five-question Northwest Hydraulic test, while Financial Reviewers (FRs) audit the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, proxy salary base calculations, specified employee limits, and subsection 78(4) and 127(26) unpaid expense accruals. In contrast, Revenu Québec administers Québec corporate income tax (Form CO-17) and Québec R&D tax incentives independently from the CRA, requiring a separate provincial corporate return, while Alberta Treasury Board and Finance administers the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) and the Innovation Employment Grant (AT1 Schedule 29) on a dual-window basis harmonized with federal SR&ED expenditure eligibility.
The April 1, 2026 CRA Administrative Modernization: Pre-Claim Approval and AI Triage

Historically, the federal SR&ED program operated strictly on a post-filing review basis, creating working-capital uncertainty for claimants whose refunds were withheld pending technical and financial audits lasting 180 days or more. As announced in Budget 2025 and implemented into SR&ED program operations as of April 1, 2026, the CRA introduced three transformative administrative reforms. First, the CRA established an elective pre-claim approval process that provides participating businesses with an up-front technical approval of their eligible SR&ED projects prior to filing the corporate tax return. Second, for SR&ED claims submitted through this elective pre-claim approval process that subsequently require an expenditure review, the CRA cut its processing time standard in half from 180 days to 90 days. Third, the CRA expanded the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) within its administrative risk-assessment pipeline to prevent low-risk SR&ED claims from being subjected to unnecessary audit interventions, while simultaneously streamlining the review process and initiating targeted consultations to simplify Form T661.
The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule 31 (along with applicable provincial schedules such as Ontario Schedule 566 and BC Schedule 425) containing all prescribed project and financial information no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred. Because a Canadian corporation's standard T2 filing deadline is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the statutory SR&ED filing deadline falls exactly 12 months after the T2 corporate return due date. This 18-month deadline is a strict statutory bar rather than a discretionary administrative guideline; neither the Minister of National Revenue nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses authority to extend the 18-month limit for prescribed SR&ED forms. If a claimant fails to submit a complete Form T661 and Schedule 31 on or before the 18-month statutory deadline, the underlying expenditures are permanently barred from entering the subsection 37(1) SR&ED deduction pool and the corporation forfeits 100% of its federal and harmonized provincial SR&ED tax credits for that taxation year.
Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Conclusions

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026—retroactively doubling the enhanced 35% federal SR&ED expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% credit to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring capital and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024—fundamentally reshapes the tax planning calculus for R&D-intensive enterprises operating in Canada. Simultaneously, Québec's abolition of five legacy R&D credits (including the Form RD-1029.7 salary credit) for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, in favour of the unified 20%/30% tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization (CRIC), integrates capital property acquisitions and pre-commercialization activities directly into the provincial credit base.

To maximize statutory entitlements while maintaining audit-ready compliance across federal and provincial jurisdictions, corporate tax directors and R&D leaders must align compensation, capital budgeting, and engineering documentation with these updated statutory rules. Specifically, because subsection 37(9) disallows bonuses and profit-based remuneration for specified employees (10% or more shareholders) and subsection 248(1) excludes dividends, innovative startups must compensate technical founders via regular periodic payroll salary calibrated against the 2026 YMPE ($74,600), recognizing that while direct SR&ED salary is capped at 5 × YMPE ($373,000) under subsection 37(9.1), the Proxy Method salary base caps a specified employee at the lesser of 75% of total regular salary and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500) under Regulation 2900(7). Furthermore, with post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases used more than 50% but less than 90% for SR&ED now claimable at 50% on Line 355 under the Proxy Method (excluding general purpose office equipment or furniture) and at actual SR&ED share on Line 360 under the Traditional Method, claimants investing heavily in shared-use laboratory, manufacturing, or AI compute infrastructure must run dual computations prior to locking in their irrevocable election on Line 160 or Line 162 of Form T661. Finally, corporations undertaking high-value experimental development projects should leverage the CRA's April 1, 2026 elective pre-claim technical approval process to secure up-front project validation and lock in the accelerated 90-day financial review processing window, while anchoring every claimed labour hour, cloud compute log, and material outlay to dated, contemporaneous records of formulated hypotheses, experimental test protocols, and analytical conclusions in accordance with Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, Manning Canning Kitchens (2025), and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175).
